title: Robust Recovery for Stochastic Block Models
authors: Jingqiu Ding (ETH Zurich, Switzerland), Tommaso D'Orsi (ETH Zurich, Switzerland), Rajai Nasser (ETH Zurich, Switzerland), David Steurer (ETH Zurich, Switzerland)
abstract: We develop an efficient algorithm for weak recovery in a robust version of the stochastic block model. The algorithm matches the statistical guarantees of the best known algorithms for the vanilla version of the stochastic block model. In this sense, our results show that there is no price of robustness in the stochastic block model. Our work is heavily inspired by recent work of Banks, Mohanty, and Raghavendra (SODA 2021) that provided an efficient algorithm for the corresponding distinguishing problem. Our algorithm and its analysis significantly depart from previous ones for robust recovery. A key challenge is the peculiar optimization landscape underlying our algorithm: The planted partition may be far from optimal in the sense that completely unrelated solutions could achieve the same objective value. This phenomenon is related to the push-out effect at the BBP phase transition for PCA. To the best of our knowledge, our algorithm is the first to achieve robust recovery in the presense of such a push-out effect in a non-asymptotic setting. Our algorithm is an instantiation of a framework based on convex optimization (related to but distinct from sum-of-squares), which may be useful for other robust matrix estimation problems. A by-product of our analysis is a general technique that boosts the probability of success (over the randomness of the input) of an arbitrary robust weak-recovery algorithm from constant (or slowly vanishing) probability to exponentially high probability.

Abstract—We develop an efﬁcient algorithm for weak recovery in a robust version of the stochastic block model.
The algorithm matches the statistical guarantees of the best
known algorithms for the vanilla version of the stochastic block
model. In this sense, our results show that there is no price of
robustness in the stochastic block model.
Our work is heavily inspired by recent work of Banks,
Mohanty, and Raghavendra (SODA 2021) that provided an
efﬁcient algorithm for the corresponding distinguishing problem.
Our algorithm and its analysis signiﬁcantly depart from
previous ones for robust recovery. A key challenge is the
peculiar optimization landscape underlying our algorithm: The
planted partition may be far from optimal in the sense that
completely unrelated solutions could achieve the same objective
value. This phenomenon is related to the push-out effect at the
BBP phase transition for PCA. To the best of our knowledge,
our algorithm is the ﬁrst to achieve robust recovery in the
presense of such a push-out effect in a non-asymptotic setting.
Our algorithm is an instantiation of a framework based
on convex optimization (related to but distinct from sumof-squares), which may be useful for other robust matrix
estimation problems.
A by-product of our analysis is a general technique that
boosts the probability of success (over the randomness of the
input) of an arbitrary robust weak-recovery algorithm from
constant (or slowly vanishing) probability to exponentially high
probability.

Robustness: A fascinating issue that arises in the
context of the works on weak recovery is robustness: The
algorithms used to show that weak recovery is possible
when 𝑑 > 4/𝜀2 are fragile in the sense that adversarially
modifying a vanishing fraction of edges could fool the

the true labels. The reason is that these algorithms are
based on particular kinds of random walks (self-avoiding
or non-backtracking) that can be affected disproportionally
by adding small cliques or other dense subgraphs.
Indeed, other kinds of algorithms (based on semideﬁnite
programming) have stronger guarantees in robust settings
[6], [7]. However, these kinds of algorithms are only known
to work for 𝑑 > 𝐶 · 4/𝜀2 for an absolute constant 𝐶 > 1

I. I NTRODUCTION
The stochastic block model is an extensively studied
statistical model for community detection in graphs. (For
a broad overview, see the excellent survey [1].) In its
most basic form, the stochastic block model describes the
following joint distribution (x, G) ∼ SBM𝑛 (𝑑, 𝜀) between a
vector 𝑥 of 𝑛 binary1 labels and an 𝑛-vertex graph G:
• draw a vector x ∈ {±1} 𝑛 uniformly at random,
• for every pair of distinct vertices 𝑖, 𝑗 ∈ [𝑛], independently create an edge {𝑖, 𝑗} in the graph G with
probability (1 + 2𝜀 · x𝑖 · x 𝑗 ) · 𝑛𝑑 .

Taken together these results raise the question whether, at
the threshold 𝑑 > 4/𝜀2 , it is inherently impossible to achieve
weak recovery robustly. Indeed, certain strong adversarial
models (“monotone adversaries”5 ) were shown to change
the threshold and require a bound of the form 𝑑 > 𝐶 · 4/𝜀2
for 𝐶 > 1 to ensure that weak recovery remains possible [9].
However, for a natural class of adversaries that are allowed
to alter any vanishing fraction of edges, it remained open
whether the threshold for weak recovery changes, or whether
weak recovery robust against this class of adversaries is
possible. In the asymptotic setting 𝑑 → ∞, this kind of robustness was achieved using the basic semideﬁnite programming relaxation for the likelihood maximization problem [8].
However, non-rigorous statistical-physics calculations [10]
suggest that the same algorithm cannot achieve the threshold
for constant degree parameter 𝑑.
Groundbreaking recent work [11] developed a
polynomial-time algorithm for the corresponding
distinguishing problem: Given a graph drawn from
SBM𝑛 (𝑑, 𝜀) with 𝑑 > 4/𝜀2 and an Erdős-Rényi random
graph with the same expected number of edges, the
algorithm can distinguish between the two graphs and
robustly so, i.e., even after altering a small constant fraction
of edges. Similarly to previous algorithms achieving the
threshold 𝑑 > 4/𝜀2 , the algorithm takes into account certain
kinds of random walks (speciﬁcally non-backtracking ones).
A crucial difference is that the algorithm considers only
walks of constant length (for ﬁxed 𝑑 and 𝜀) as opposed
to walks of logarithmic length like previous algorithms. In
order to leverage the more limited information provided
by shorter walks, the algorithm in [11] needs to employ
heavier convex optimization techniques (speciﬁcally sumof-squares). The upside is that robustness follows almost
directly: The altered edges can affect only a small constant
fraction of the (constant-length) walks considered by the
algorithm. Correspondingly, the effect on the optimal value
for the optimization is small.
